headline: Garment unrest clouds fragile economic recovery as factories close
summary: Wage protests enter a fourth day, forcing hundreds of factories to shut down while economic data shows uneven growth and record-low private sector credit.
details: Wage protests by garment workers have entered a fourth day, forcing several hundred factories to close. This unrest comes as fresh economic data reveals a fragile and uneven recovery for Bangladesh.

In the first four months of the fiscal year, exports grew by 6 percent and remittances by 13 percent. However, private sector credit growth fell to a record low of 4.17 percent in September, signaling weak investment.
Economists warn that prolonged unrest in the garment sector could further weaken the economy by disrupting production and threatening buyer confidence and delivery commitments.
Mustafizur Rahman of the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) noted that while exports and reserves have performed relatively well, inflation remains stubbornly high at around 8.5 percent.
Ashikur Rahman of the Policy Research Institute of Bangladesh highlighted that credit growth is contracting in real terms because it is growing more slowly than inflation.
Experts suggest that credible dialogue to address workers' wage and cost-of-living concerns is essential to protecting livelihoods and maintaining export competitiveness.
Other recommended reforms include stabilizing foreign exchange reserves, reducing non-performing loans in the banking sector, and ensuring uninterrupted power and gas supplies for industries.
caption:
Hundreds of garment factories shut down as wage protests enter day four. Is the economic recovery at risk?

Wage protests by garment workers have entered a fourth day, forcing several hundred factories to close. This unrest comes as fresh economic data reveals a fragile and uneven recovery for Bangladesh.

In the first four months of the fiscal year, exports grew by 6 percent and remittances by 13 percent. However, private sector credit growth fell to a record low of 4.17 percent in September, signaling weak investment.

Economists warn that prolonged unrest in the garment sector could further weaken the economy by disrupting production and threatening buyer confidence and delivery commitments.

Mustafizur Rahman of the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) noted that while exports and reserves have performed relatively well, inflation remains stubbornly high at around 8.5 percent.

Ashikur Rahman of the Policy Research Institute of Bangladesh highlighted that credit growth is contracting in real terms because it is growing more slowly than inflation.

Experts suggest that credible dialogue to address workers' wage and cost-of-living concerns is essential to protecting livelihoods and maintaining export competitiveness.

Other recommended reforms include stabilizing foreign exchange reserves, reducing non-performing loans in the banking sector, and ensuring uninterrupted power and gas supplies for industries.

topic: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case
headline_marked: ICJ to [[deliver ruling on Rohingya genocide case]] on Nov 19
headline: ICJ to deliver ruling on Rohingya genocide case on Nov 19
summary: The World Court will decide if Myanmar's 2017 military crackdown on the Rohingya people resulted in genocide.
details: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has set November 19 as the date for its judgment on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority.
The case was brought by The Gambia in 2019, alleging that the 2017 military offensive against the Rohingya amounted to genocide.
The 2017 crackdown forced at least 730,000 people to flee their homes and seek refuge in Bangladesh.
Rohingya refugees have reported widespread killings, mass rape, and arson during the military operation.
Myanmar denies the allegations, claiming its military operation was a legitimate counter-terrorism campaign.
This ruling will be only the third time the ICJ has ever delivered a judgment in a genocide case and is the first such ruling in over a decade.
The outcome could influence future international legal proceedings, including South Africa's case against Israel regarding Gaza.
The ICJ, known as the World Court, is the UN's highest judicial body and settles disputes between states based on international treaties like the 1948 Genocide Convention.
caption:
A landmark ruling on the Rohingya genocide case is coming. The World Court will deliver its judgment on November 19.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has set November 19 as the date for its judgment on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority.

The case was brought by The Gambia in 2019, alleging that the 2017 military offensive against the Rohingya amounted to genocide.

The 2017 crackdown forced at least 730,000 people to flee their homes and seek refuge in Bangladesh.

Rohingya refugees have reported widespread killings, mass rape, and arson during the military operation.

Myanmar denies the allegations, claiming its military operation was a legitimate counter-terrorism campaign.

This ruling will be only the third time the ICJ has ever delivered a judgment in a genocide case and is the first such ruling in over a decade.

The outcome could influence future international legal proceedings, including South Africa's case against Israel regarding Gaza.

The ICJ, known as the World Court, is the UN's highest judicial body and settles disputes between states based on international treaties like the 1948 Genocide Convention.
